speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: Under this Act, employers have to offer re-employment to eligible employees up to the age of 65.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: If the employer is unable to do so, he has to offer an Employment Assistance Payment (EAP) to the employees to tide them over the period when they are looking for alternative employment.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: One key feature of re-employment is that it need not be for the same job or on the same terms.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: Both the employer and the employee can consult each other and work out mutually agreeable arrangements.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: Both parties have the flexibility to make changes to the existing job arrangements to suit their needs.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: Re-employment, therefore, balances the objectives of providing opportunities for employees to work longer on the one hand, while maintaining some flexibility for the employers on the other.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: The introduction of re-employment in 2012, coupled with the efforts from the tripartite partners to encourage age-friendly workplaces, has made a positive impact on the employment of older Singaporeans.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: In 2015, over 98% of private sector local employees who wished to continue working at the age of 62 were offered re-employment.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: Ninety-eight percent of those who accepted re-employment in the same job also did not experience any cut in their basic wages.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: Five years on from 2012, which is 2017 now, Singapore's workforce continues to age.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: Over the last decade, the proportion of residents aged 60 and above in our labour force has increased from 5.5% in 2006 to 12% in 2015.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: As we live longer, we can expect this proportion to continue to grow.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: The intention to raise the re-employment age to 67 was already announced in 2012.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: Since then, after extensive consultation and negotiation, the tripartite partners have agreed that we are now ready to take this next step.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: This Bill makes three key changes to the Retirement and Re-employment Act.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: Second, we will introduce a new option to allow re-employment by another employer.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: Third, we will remove the existing option of employers to cut wages of employees at age 60.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: Eligible employees, who are locals with at least satisfactory work performance and who are medically fit, should be offered re-employment until age 67.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: This is what the tripartite partners agreed to after extensive consultations.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: This is on top of the SEC of up to 8% for employing Singaporeans aged 55 and above.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: This additional wage offset will expire on 1 July 2017.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: The Government is studying the need and manner to further extend it to encourage voluntary re-employment for two groups of Singaporean employees.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: First, those aged below 67 but not covered by the new re-employment age of 67.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: Second, those beyond the new re-employment age of 67.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: We are aware that older employees and their employers need clarity on the future of the scheme.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: A decision will be taken well ahead of the expiration of the current scheme.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: The second key change is to allow eligible employees to be re-employed by another employer to increase options for both the employers and the employees.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: Some of these employers would like to help their older employees secure re-employment with another employer.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: However, today's law does not allow them to transfer their re-employment obligations to another employer.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: So, from 1 July 2017, the law will allow an employer, who is unable to offer a suitable position in his own organisation, to transfer his re-employment obligations to another employer.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: The original employer will be deemed as having fulfilled his re-employment obligations.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: The employee will have more opportunities to be re-employed and will enjoy re-employment protection under the second employer.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: The second employer will likewise benefit from hiring an employee with experience.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: There will be safeguards put in place to protect these employees.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: The employee has to agree to the re-employment terms with the second employer, and the second employer has to agree to take over all applicable obligations and re-employment obligations for this employee.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: If either condition is not met, the original employer still has to fulfil his re-employment obligations.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: This means that the original employer still has to offer EAP if he cannot find a job for the older employee in his own company.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: To prepare employers and employees for these changes, we have worked with the tripartite partners to revise the Tripartite Guidelines on the Re-employment of Older Employees.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: In particular, we added a new section on re-employment by a new employer to provide guidance on this new option.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: My Ministry will be issuing the revised Guidelines later today.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: This will take effect on 1 July 2017.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: Employers and employees who require more information may direct their queries to the Ministry of Manpower (MOM), the Singapore National Employers Federation (SNEF) or the National Trades Union Congress (NTUC).

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: In 1999, this option was introduced to help employers with seniority-based wage systems to manage their wage costs when the retirement age was raised from 60 to 62.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: Since then, with the restructuring and reshaping of Singapore's economy, tripartite efforts have been successful in moving employers away from seniority-based wage systems.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Besides this extension, two other key amendments will be effected.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: The extension of the re-employment age is a welcome move by our unions, union leaders, union members and workers as this is what the Labour Movement has been lobbying for.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: This issue is of urgency and importance, especially with our ageing populace, as it will provide our workers who are keen and able to continue working the opportunity to be re-employed until the age of 67.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: I applaud the tripartite partners for their untiring efforts in reviewing and improving the current Act.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: This set of amendments and the upcoming tripartite guidelines were arrived at through heavy discussions and robust negotiations and will benefit all employees, whether low-wage workers or professionals, managers and executives (PMEs).

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Although this deck of amendments is a positive step forward, how it is executed and rolled out is vital.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: I ask that the respective tripartite partners play their part to ensure its success.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: On the part of employers, with our tight labour market and stagnating employment growth, employers play the most important role in having not just fair but progressive practices in the hiring of the not-so-young workers, especially the re-employment of workers.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: In my regular ground engagements with workers, especially PMEs, I still hear of instances where workers are confronted with ageism.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Although not rampant and good work has been done by the Tripartite Alliance for Fair Employment Practices (TAFEP), I believe we can do more to not just minimise but eradicate all forms of ageism.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Employers must actively invest in re-thinking how best to re-deploy their mature workers to fully leverage their expertise.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: It is also imperative for employers to re-design the job and/or workplace to make the job easier, safer and smarter for our ageing workforce.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: This can be achieved by embracing disruption, technology and innovation through recreating jobs and building up a quality workforce so as to increase productivity and achieve inclusive quality growth.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: EAP has to be regularly reviewed upwards to keep pace with rising median wages.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: EAP amounts and abuse must be closely watched and not become an easy tool or a backdoor exploited by employers as an easy way out to absolve themselves of their obligation to re-employ.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: I urge MOM to also pay a close watch on any cases of abuse or indiscriminate utilisation of the new provision where employers can transfer the re-employment obligation to another employer and discharge themselves of responsibility.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: This is especially so when the terms, conditions, environment and nature of work in the new job may vastly differ from what they had been previously employed for.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Workers, too, must play their part by preparing for re-employment and have to continue to do their part to stay ready, relevant and resilient: ready with new skills, relevant to the new jobs and also resilient to new changes.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: We must move away from re-employment for the sake of statutory compliance to people development, productivity growth and taking active steps to change stereotypical perceptions on age, talent, productivity and compensation in every organisation.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: I want to make a special call for our tripartite partners to work closely together to ensure the spirit and intent of these amendments are executed well and thoroughly so as to achieve their desired outcomes.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: More importantly, society plays the most crucial role in how we, as one community and one country, view and treat older workers and embrace an ageing population.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Not just acknowledging and accommodating the ageing workforce but proactively accepting and appreciating every worker regardless of age!

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Mindsets of our tripartite partners as well as society need to change.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: My colleague, Assoc Prof Daniel Goh, will speak more broadly about this Bill.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The language of clause 4, Part I, suggests that this is the case since it states that notwithstanding any law, contract of service or collective agreement, the retirement age should not be less than 62 years and up to 67 years, as prescribed by the Minister.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Section 4, Part II, of the existing Act also says that no employer shall dismiss on the ground of age any employee who is below 62 years of age or the prescribed minimum retirement age.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: However, this makes it all the more likely that an employer who is terminating an employee for reasons of ageism will not tell this to the employee or leave any paper trail as to the grounds for the termination.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: There are two scenarios I would like to highlight here.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The first is that of an employer who does not wish to offer re-employment on grounds of performance, which is allowed under the Bill, and the second is that of an employer who terminates an employee with notice on ageist grounds because they have become too old but does not state this reason or leave any evidence of this being the reason.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It would seem to be an escape clause for the employer who wants to invoke the retirement age against the reluctant employee and not offer her re-employment.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Take, for example, their performance was satisfactory or if the reasonable notice was not provided.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: To be realistic, if an employer does not offer re-employment on grounds of performance, it may be hard for many employees to defend themselves to MOM, particularly if the company does not practise a system of regular performance reviews with documentary proof of the same, which is the case with many small and medium enterprises (SMEs).

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The second scenario I would like to discuss is even more likely and, hence, even more worrying.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: What if an employer decides to terminate an employee just before she hits the age of 62 or even earlier, on the grounds of ageist prejudice, without invoking the reason of retirement at all, or without invoking the reason of age at all, but simply because they have decided that they can hire someone younger and more cheaply?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: There may be safeguards against employers doing this in the case of companies that have collective bargaining employment contracts.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But most employees do not fall into this category.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: For most employees, there is no need for an employer to wait for the retirement age or re-employment age.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Legally, they can terminate an employee with notice at any time.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In other words, they can involuntarily retire their employees as and when they feel they have become too old.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: For most employees, there is no protection against such termination with notice or reasons of ageist prejudice unless it is very easy to prove that.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This is because the law does not require the employer to state the reason nor is it easily challenged at MOM if the termination is a legal employment contract termination with notice period paid.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: To be sure, I am not arguing that employers should have the ability to terminate with notice eliminated.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Employers need to be able to eliminate unnecessary positions as a last resort so as to protect the survival of the company and the jobs of the remaining workers under certain circumstances.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Employers also need this in cases of legitimate employee performance issues.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: My concern is with employers who exercise this right for the wrong reasons − for reasons of ageist prejudice.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: No doubt, this is an issue that goes beyond the scope of the current changes to the Act and touches on our framework for dealing with discriminatory employment practices in general.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But it is worth noting that this law does not address this possibility.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It is a possibility that faces a huge number of workers who may be forcibly retired and, hence, thrown onto a job market where finding good permanent employment for someone in their late 40s or 50s, let alone older, is extremely hard, especially in the current economic climate.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This points to a huge gap which the law does not address.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I suspect that many of these workers would have undergone countless ordeals of sending in applications with no reply, or going for interviews only to be met with rejections or a stone wall of silence until they decided to give up the unequal struggle.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: A good starting point would be to get good data from a comprehensive survey of employees, not only of employers, and this is a subject we have discussed in this House last year.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We could then look at better carrots for employers who can demonstrate robust and auditable hiring and firing practices that give no quarter to prejudice of any kind.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Further down the road, depending on the effectiveness of these measures, as surveys reveal, we could consider introducing sticks against proven and repeated discriminators, as my colleague Mr Faisal Manap argued during the 2016 Committee of Supply debate.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Such work opens up a crucial vista for self-fulfilment for older Singaporeans who might otherwise be at risk of social isolation.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It also gives older people a fair chance to enhance their incomes by earning an honest pay.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: As a country, it allows us to raise our total labour force participation and thus staff our industries without adding to the population as much.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: To move down this path, we need to go much further than this Bill.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: However, I strongly believe that it is necessary at this point in time to speak up about the challenges I believe it brings to the economy.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: Until fairly recently, the combination of increasing foreign manpower levies and tighter quota restrictions appeared to have done little to slake the seemingly insatiable appetite of employers for manpower.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: It was not so long ago that the labour market was assessed to still to be tight and employers bemoaned the impact of unfilled vacancies on their capacity to meet robust demand.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: The apparent change in the labour market did not occur overnight.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: The shifting sands of the global economic landscape, accentuated by volatile energy price movements and trade flows, are nothing new.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: But what has added to the uncertainty are the disruptive outcomes of high-profile events over the past year.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: These events hold significant consequences for future trends in global trade, upon which Singapore depends so critically.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: Singapore has not been slow to anticipate the need to be prepared for such "Black Swan" events.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: Since the crisis of 2008/2009, the labour market has been undergoing deep change, reorienting away from excessive reliance on foreign manpower.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: One prominent result of this reorientation is the remarkable increase in the labour force participation rate (LFPR).

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: The increase in the resident LFPR in recent years has been especially pronounced for two groups, namely, females and older workers.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: A large share of the credit for this goes to the concerted efforts made by our Government policymakers to expand employment opportunities.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: And in order to effect real changes, these efforts have not been sudden nor impulsive, but instead, were implemented in a calibrated fashion over a period of time in order to ensure that relevant stakeholders have time to buy into the changes.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: So, instead of simply raising the retirement age, what the Government has opted to do is to expand re-employment opportunities.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: Everyone's ideal is for workers who are willing and able to work productively to do so without being asked to retire.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: The retirement age has served to deal with this difficult question all these years, and we will have to take a long, hard look at the deeper implications of doing away with retirement altogether.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: In the meantime, given the potential implications of raising the retirement age, it makes sense to focus instead on re-employment.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: Hence, I support the Government's efforts in this push.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: But if we take into account the current economic climate, the changes proposed in this Bill have certain important implications.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: Raising the retirement age and facilitating re-employment opportunities seem to be natural options to take as a follow-up to the success in raising the resident LFPR, but it is important to recognise that the situation is a lot less straightforward because the impact varies with different groups of workers and different types of employers.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: There are many reasons why it is important to expand the opportunities for older persons to work, if they wish to.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: Foremost among these, of course, is the ageing population, as the Minister has already mentioned.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: In addition, MOM's  statistics report that older residents aged 60 and over accounted for the largest share among age groups with residents outside the labour force.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: However, the raising of the re-employment age is just one factor which will tackle this issue.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: Another important factor is the duration of the employment contracts that employees are on.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: So, despite the improvement over the intervening period of time, the age-connected pattern in term contracts has remained basically unchanged.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: Hence, just as in June 2007, the proportion of employees on term contracts was more than twice that of all other age groups for those above 24 years of age.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: In addition, the proportion of resident employees on term contracts was lowest for those aged 30 to 39, and then increased with the group age thereafter for all the other groups.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: As MOM had noted in the past in its 2006 Labour Market report, and I quote, "the incidence of contract employment was higher among the younger and older employees, including those on casual or on-call employment, and was mainly concentrated in the lower skilled jobs, such as cleaning and labouring, sales and service and clerical work." The reality is that this characterisation remains largely valid today.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: Is there a concern, therefore, that with the obligations imposed by the re-employment legislation that we see now, more employers may be driven by the strain of the regulatory burden to prefer placing older employees on term contracts?

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: Re-employment is dependent on employers being in a position of operating health and having the means to retain older workers.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: Availability of older workers benefit employers by expanding the size of the labour pool.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: At the same time, they increase competition for jobs.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: This is why flexibility from both employers and employees is needed in agreeing on re-employment terms.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: Significant emphasis on such flexibility was placed on this in the Tripartite Guidelines on the Re-employment of Older Employees that was released in January 2011.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: Here, I would like to thank MOM for helping to clarify that the repeal of section 5 is not related to the re-employment contract.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: Nonetheless, section 5 could have been seen, correctly or not, as impacting overall salary adjustments.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: I support the decision to repeal section 5.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: The problem with it is that although it has limited salary cuts of 10%, it was never completely clear, to me at least, whether the limit is taken into account later as part of total adjustments that would be due to job changes agreed in a re-employment contract.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: In the longer term, Madam, I believe that these changes are sound.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: But at the present moment, however, it is not entirely clear what lies ahead for the labour market as the economy confronts the current bout of weakness.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: We should consider whether we are loading too much on to the economy by expecting it to deliver on multiple fronts, without allowing it more time to adjust at a pace more suited to accommodating the seismic shifts it is experiencing.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: One major concern I have about "hardwiring" the obligations of employers further is that it may become an additional burden on them when economic conditions weaken, as we could be seeing.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: Over the last few years, the labour market has held up well, due in no small part to the support of various schemes, some of which the Minister has already mentioned.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: The re-employment push is currently receiving very strong support from the tripartite partners.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: On its part, in addition to transforming mindsets through its own re-employment practices, the Government also offers substantial wage support through the payment of a Special Employment Credit.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: In other words, companies which need to generate jobs are themselves under severe pressure.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: The heavy reliance on wage support in recent years could have come at a price.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: Going forward, the scope for using further wage support to make up for weak labour market demand is diminished, I believe, because they have been in force for some time.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: If employment conditions weaken further, a heavily legislated employment regime may increase the difficulty that companies face in trying to manoeuvre their way out of a business trough.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: Why do companies need more room to manoeuvre?

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: There are many signs that the economic conditions of the future will not be the same uniform challenge to all, as we have seen in the past, but could instead consist of a variegated landscape.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: At the same time that we see some businesses doing very well, others could face substantially different and very difficult competitive circumstances.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: As a commentator for the Business Times appeared to suggest last week, and I agree strongly, it could simply be because such companies operate at the confluence of disruptive new phenomena.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: America's economic recovery has been replete with such examples over the last few years.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: Just days ago, at the same time that jobs growth in the US is returning to health, Macy's, an American chain, announced store closures and worker layoffs.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: This type of phenomenon is part of the new normal, and we have to help our companies in Singapore compete, reorganise and, if necessary, resurrect themselves with all the room to manoeuvre that is necessary.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: Because at the end of the day, we still rely on healthy businesses to create good jobs.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: If we take size, for instance, a large organisation with a strong human resource structure will be able to incorporate some of the changes that are required under the new legislative framework readily with possibly negligible additional costs, compared to a business with a very small number of employees.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: Will a small business be given time to set up processes, such as an employee performance evaluation system, in order to comply with the requirement on assessing the eligibility for re-employment?

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: On a related note, I would also like to ask about the quantum of the EAP.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: With the current economic climate placing employers under strain as well, this could add pressure to those already in difficulty.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: As Singapore's labour market prepares to adjust to a different set of circumstances in future, I believe that leadership from the tripartite partners in empathising with one another's position will continue to be a much-needed ingredient.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: But it may still fall short if we look at the life expectancy trends in Singapore and other parts of the world.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Increasing life expectancy is a global phenomenon, and studies showed that it would increase, on average, by 2.5 years for every decade, three months per year or six hours per day.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: In fact, for millennial babies born in early 2000 onwards, half of them can live beyond 100 years.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: On average, we are looking at Singaporeans' life expectancy increasing by 3.5 years for every decade.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Like other developed countries, half of our millennial babies will live beyond 100 years.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Even those Singaporeans born after 1965, half of them will live past 90 years old.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: If our workforce is living up to 100 years, it means that we have to work longer or save more.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Given the future's reality, our retirement age must increase over time, to perhaps, 70 to 75 years to ensure a steady income stream for livelihood.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Alternatively, we should not look at a single retirement age but maybe a retirement age based on age cohort.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: In time to come, we need to be bolder to work towards removing the retirement age and allow a worker to work as long as he or she could.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Nevertheless, I still support this Bill amendment as a step in the right direction.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Given this amendment in the Bill, I would like to suggest the Ministry monitor this new re-employment provision to closely assess its practicality and make future refinements to ensure effectiveness.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: That said, there are some areas I would like to touch on with regard to this Bill.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: There should be some provisions for EAP to be paid by the first employer to assist the employee if the second does not extend the contract into the second year on unfair grounds.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This will prevent any possible collusion or even uncertainties on the part of our older workforce, which can be very detrimental to their well-being and motivation.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: For example, the employer can arbitrarily choose not to offer re-employment to the employee if the employee is assessed by his employer to have unsatisfactory work performance or is medically unfit to continue working.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The law should make provisions to allow for a worker to have independent assessment on medical fitness.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This can be achieved by appointing a review panel of independent doctors to challenge the assessment of the company's doctor when the worker is certified unfit to work.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: If he is reassessed and deemed actually to be fit, and the company has no vacancies, he should have a form of recourse through EAP.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Thirdly, there should be tripartite guidelines issued for the employer to communicate to the affected employee on his plans to transfer re-employment obligations to a second employer.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This process of matching should ideally begin a year prior to the date of the employee's re-employment to also allow him to make better decisions.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The nature and scope of the alternative job should also be deliberated with the worker.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This will make for a more streamlined and consistent approach to the transferring of re-employment obligations.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This can still be subject to valuations on performance and health check as well.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Besides the above changes, the law can also look into providing incentives for companies that can strategically map out a second career for employees as early as 45 years into their lives.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This foresight will allow companies to plan ahead, both for their own companies and for their own employees.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This increases the likelihood of ensuring that their employees can carry skills that are relevant not just to their companies, but also to the industry as a whole.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: (In Malay):   While the amendment to this Bill will extend the re-employment age to 67, it does not guarantee that a job will be available to the worker.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Although this amendment has provisions for a worker to find a job with an alternative employer or be provided a higher EAP, the worker will have a better chance to continue working until 67 years old if the worker constantly ensures that he/she upgrades to the relevant skills through lifelong learning.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Regardless of whether a person is in a low-paying or high-paying job, the chances of re-employment will be lesser without the relevant knowledge and skills to make the person employable.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Hence, it is important that such training support programmes be constantly updated and frequently reviewed to ensure that those programmes will complement this Bill.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: (In English): Madam, the effectiveness of this Bill requires every party to do its part.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: If we get it right, it will be a real gift; to ignore and fail to prepare will be a curse." Mdm Speaker, I support the amendments to the Bill.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: How many senior Singaporeans who had wanted to work longer have lost many good working years as a result?

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I sincerely hope it was not due to the political calculation of electoral cycles.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If not, what were the demographic and economic considerations underlying the long delay to raise the retirement age to 67?

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Government owes Singaporeans an explanation because during these 23 years, we saw a massive influx of foreign mid-skilled workers who out-competed senior Singaporeans in the labour market.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It was also during these 23 years that we saw a culture of ageism take root, so much so that analysts, unionists, Government leaders and Members of this House have been calling for a mindset change among employers to change their attitude towards senior workers.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Habits and norms, once settled in place, are very difficult to change.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In this case, policy inaction has allowed the culture of ageism to deepen and shape society's view that senior workers are less valuable than younger workers.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The benefits of allowing senior Singaporeans to continue to work go beyond the narrow dollar and cents of economic value.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: A study by researchers at the Singapore Institute of Management (SIM) University in 2013 shows many benefits.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Work gives senior Singaporeans a sense of social purpose as they feel that they are doing something useful for others and society.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Work is also a recognition that they are still valued by others and society.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Work provides for a sense of autonomy, as they have the opportunity to deploy their skills and solve problems.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Work provides for positive relationships as many senior Singaporeans make good friends at their workplaces.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: For the senior Singaporeans themselves, many would like to continue working to remain financially independent, to be socially integrated, to maintain good health and for self-fulfilment.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If we consider the qualitative benefits of work, beyond the quantitative measures of a narrow economic model, allowing senior Singaporeans to work longer kills many birds with one stone.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It helps with the retirement insecurity of inadequate CPF savings.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It helps to push back the onset of dementia and other ageing health issues.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It helps to improve the psychological well-being of senior Singaporeans and enhances ageing in place, as the workplace is also a meaningful social place for senior Singaporeans.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Getting the right retirement age policy to facilitate senior Singaporeans to continue to work is not just an economic issue.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It will tackle with one stone the many issues related to the ageing population.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: However, that one stone has to be thrown right and accurate.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We have no more time to waste with the ageing society at our doorstep.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: What we have here is a throw of a stone that is still too tentative.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In this regard, I have six points to raise for the Minister to address and consider.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The first point, why is 67 the magic number after more than two decades?

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Today's average life expectancy is around 83 years and still rising.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: What was the model that was used to calculate the optimal retirement age that led to 67 as the target retirement age in 1993?

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Should the effective retirement age not be adjusted as life expectancy goes up?

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Should it not be around 70 years of age today?

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The larger point is the automatic linking of effective retirement age to life expectancy, which is the emerging best practice in developed economies around the world.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This is so that the financial risks of ageing could be more equitably borne by all sectors of society, especially employers.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Would the Government consider this policy innovation and link the effective retirement age to life expectancy, since we have now reached the target age of 67?

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The second point: is the retirement age going to be stuck at 62?

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Twenty years is a good time to reconsider whether we should raise the retirement age to 65 for future cohorts and existing cohorts if they so desire.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This will encourage employers to think longer term when it comes to staff recruitment and, especially, training and retention.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It would also give greater job security to Singaporeans and address the tight labour market conditions when we reduce the factor of foreign labour inputs.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: At the 2015 National Day Rally, when announcing that the re-employment age would be raised to 67, the Prime Minister noted that employers had gotten used to employees working to 65 and were starting to benefit from it.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If so, why not entrench 65 as the retirement age then?

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: They do not even cut salaries by 10% at age 60 anymore, which is why the Bill is repealing that part of the law.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Is there any reason why the Government would not do this?

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The third point, in the extension of the re-employment age to 67, this Bill could have dealt with one of the biggest issues faced by senior workers who want to continue to work − the short-term length of their annual contracts.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The one-year term contract or a three-year contract to be reviewed yearly sustains a sense of insecurity about contract review and renewal, which is not the right way to treat a senior employee and colleague.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Is there any reason not to stipulate the contract length to be at least two years, unless the senior chooses otherwise to have one-year contracts?

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It makes more sense too, since employers should consider performance records of the past two to three years when re-employing senior workers.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The fourth point, there is the possibility for a loss of benefits in the switch from regular employment to the re-employment contract.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This loss of benefits while still being employed to do the same work by the same company in the same workplace with the same colleagues is solely due to the employee reaching a certain age.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Is this not unfair, smacking of ageism, and stigmatising for the senior Singaporeans?

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This has real physical consequences, too, when it comes to medical benefits.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: There is a short circuit to the current policy logic.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Employers are required to re-employ senior workers who are medically fit and yet they are allowed to reduce the medical benefits, when the benefits present a serious cost concern.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Is it not self-defeating that the reduction of medical benefits could lead to senior workers becoming medically unfit for continued re-employment?

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The fifth point, other than the criterion of medical fitness, employers are required to re-employ workers who have satisfactory work performance.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: However, for medical fitness, the Act currently has a section stating that the employee is presumed to be medically fit unless the employer proves otherwise on the balance of probabilities.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: There is no equivalent clause for the work performance eligibility criterion.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I understand there is a need to balance the interests of employers and workers and allow for enough flexibility when it comes to re-employment.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: However, what recourse does a senior worker have when the employer refuses him or her the right of re-employment on grounds of unsatisfactory work performance which the senior worker disagrees with?

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If the normal convention applies, the burden of proof is on the senior worker to show that the termination is unfair.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This is onerous and borders on the impossible for many senior workers, especially when they are not professionals, managers, executives and technicians (PMETs) who would usually have access to human resource records for formal performance reviews.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Does the Ministry depart from the convention of placing the burden of proof on the worker for senior workers seeking recourse on this matter?

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If not, would the Ministry do so for senior workers being rejected for re-employment by investigating the evidence on the balance of probabilities?

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If so, this effectively delinks the CPF LIFE minimum payout age from the re-employment age.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This means that at age 65, senior workers can enjoy monthly CPF LIFE income to augment their regular income from re-employment to 67 years of age.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Workers' Party has been calling for this delinking of the CPF drawdown age from the retirement age since the debate on CPF reforms in 2007.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: With this delinking, we are now in line with the practice of pension and retirement policy in many developed countries internationally.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: With this delinking, the Government is acknowledging that there is no need for a rigid fixing of the pension income payout age to the retirement age because there is no rigid relationship between the two.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Many developed countries allow for earlier pension income payout regardless of employment status of senior citizens, so that the seniors could start adjusting to their retirement plans even as they continue to work.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Why not allow senior workers to begin collecting their CPF LIFE payout earlier at 60 years of age if they choose to?

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This will allow them to augment their regular income earlier, which may well be critical for senior workers to maintain their good physical health so that they can be medically fit for re-employment at 62.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The only reason I can think of not allowing senior workers to start collecting their CPF LIFE payout earlier is that the Government does not trust our senior workers to use a few extra hundred dollars a month wisely by investing in their own health and in their own retirement plans, especially if they would like to continue to work.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: When it comes to the retirement and re-employment policy, we have been catering flexibility for employers to protect their bottom line for many years now.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We should also cater flexibility for employees to help them protect their financial and physical health.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: And now that it has, I have these six questions for the Government.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: One, should the Government consider linking the effective retirement age to the average life expectancy of Singaporeans?

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Three, why maintain the annual review and renewal structure of re-employment contracts?

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This tool should not be influenced by short-term economic and political concerns.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It is important for us to harness the retirement age policy for its long-term impact and implications for the ageing society.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I hope the Government will have the courage to do so even if it would prove unpopular in the short run.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Longer life expectancy and better healthcare systems have allowed workers to work longer and more productively.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: I welcome the amendments in this Bill as they will take Singapore further in providing more options for older workers and companies.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: It provides the flexibility to strike a good balance between the interests of both workers and companies.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The changes proposed in this Bill are important threads in our tapestry of support for older workers, which will take time to develop.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: This Bill is timely as it comes at a time when we need to meet the challenges of an ageing population.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: In weaving this tapestry, we must be guided by a vision of ageless workplaces.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: In such workplaces, employers and workers are not fixated on age, older workers are not seen as liabilities, and technology will better enable older workers rather than replace them.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: It is a lofty vision but it is one that is imperative for an ageing Singapore.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: It will take time, but we will get there.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: But some aspects of this Bill will have already contributed to this vision.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: I believe that we can and should do more to support the shift towards ageless workplaces.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: In this economic slowdown, we can easily lose momentum, and older workers, who are most vulnerable during restructuring, will suffer the brunt of it.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: This incentivises them to keep even more of their older, mid-level workers.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: This Bill also provides for a second employer to take over the employment terms of an older worker.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: How will the Government ensure that all means are exhausted before workers are transferred?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: What safeguards will be put in place to ensure that this does not act as a conduit for ill-intentioned companies to use the new companies to exit workers via liquidation?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: In addition, for workers who will be transferred to a new company, could the Government provide training programmes and leave support so that they can smoothly transition into their new career?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: It will be helpful to our older workers in terms of financial planning and self-fulfilment through work.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: This is an important step towards our vision of building an inclusive and ageless workforce.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The concerns of the older workers are understandable.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Many of our workers, by the time they reach the retirement age, are still unable to achieve financial freedom and have to continue to work.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: There are also many Singaporeans who would like to stay connected with society and long to continue working.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Many older Singaporeans wish to achieve a balance between work, family, aspirations and physical strength.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: However, looking for a suitable job can be a difficult and frustrating challenge.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Jobs matched and training provided will be specifically selected to suit the older workers.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: This will make things much easier for them.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Although we have legislation in place, employers and employees need to have a change of mindset and thinking to achieve our vision of building an ageless and inclusive society.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The Government and employers should work together to improve the work process and fully develop the workers' potential, and not go by the old way of recruiting foreign workers whenever there is a shortage of manpower.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Workers themselves must also be willing to try new jobs.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Only by doing this can we fundamentally eradicate age discrimination and create an inclusive society.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: (In English): Mr Deputy Speaker, please let me continue in English.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: There is a need for dedicated channels and platforms with curated silver-friendly jobs to help older workers function well in jobs that they are suited for.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: We have already done the same for PMETs.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Could we not take the same approach with our older workers so that their skills and knowledge can be tapped on in an environment that is better suited for their needs?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: After all, we must all work in the spirit of the law, rather than just the letter.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: It is unfair to a worker who does the same job to have his pay reduced once he reaches 60.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I am also happy to support the amendment which allows eligible employees to be re-employed by other employers with the older workers' consent.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This will be more flexible than the current arrangement, where the employment obligations lie with the older worker's employer.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: In the event an employer is unable to find a suitable job within his company for the older worker, he will be able to transfer him.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: However, I am concerned that it would not be easy to transfer re-employment obligations of a 67-year-old employee to another employer in practice.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The highest chances of success may be transfers to a subsidiary or related companies.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Unfortunately, most SMEs do not have this option.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: In addition, companies may face a manpower crunch which does not allow them to look into helping the older workers find suitable jobs in other companies.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This may result in the companies taking the easy way out by offering EAP which is a waste since many workers still can work and want to work.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The highest tier of SEC is 8% for employees aged 65 and above.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: While this incentive is appreciated, additional benefits would be useful.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Employers would be concerned about potential energy and declines in cognitive functions in workers in their late 60's and would need extra motivation to hire these older workers.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: (In Mandarin):   Under the Retirement and Re-employment (Amendment) Bill, if a company with older workers do not have suitable positions for employees eligible for re-employment, they may choose to arrange for them to work in other companies, including a subsidiary or related companies.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The important thing is that new employers should not just be fixated on whether the older worker can do the job.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Although that is important, employers should also ensure the older employee can adjust to the new environment and adapt because older workers take time to adapt and adjust.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: It would be best if they are made aware of the whole work environment, instead of just knowing what work they themselves will do.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I am sure that with years of experience, they can adjust appropriately and make even better contributions to the company.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We must encourage and guide Singaporeans to lifelong learning and ensure good results, so that they can cope with the challenges of new work environments.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I hope that the Government will consider providing tax incentives to employers who are willing to hire and support the training of older workers.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: MOM is amending the legislation and requesting employers to shoulder more responsibilities.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: As an employer, I support the amendment of this Bill.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: However, from the perspective of an employer, I also wish to voice some of my opinions.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: Singapore's population is gradually ageing and extending the re-employment age is a major trend.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: Older workers have a wealth of experience and, if their health conditions permit, could remain in their positions.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: This is good for the company and for the individual.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: However, we also need to understand their limitations; in particular, during the current volatile business environment, many industries are restructuring, and the Government is also encouraging businessmen to improve their productivity and lessen the reliance on workers.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: Under these circumstances, the Government is requesting employers to arrange for a position for a 62-year-old employee to work until 67, even if there is no position available.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: Frankly speaking, the Government's new request and the direction for the last few years are clearly not on the same frequency.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: People aged around 65 are the baby-boomers and constitute a substantial number.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: Before 1 July 2017, enterprises need to do proper financial planning.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: On one hand, we need to raise productivity.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: On the other hand, we need to consider the situation of older workers, who may not be able to adapt immediately to technology which is too advanced, or methods which are too trendy.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: The company's capital is a pool, and if there is some outflow here and there, and no water flows in, the pool of water would be reduced.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: The ideal scenario is to have some outflow but balanced by some inflow, and maintaining that level of water could then ensure normal operations.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: In this regard, can businessmen expect the Government to reduce other costs, like the foreign worker levy, the Certificate of Entitlement for commercial vehicles or, as the Member has just mentioned, offer more tax rebates to bring down their newly-added expenses?

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: A company can only look after its older workers well if the company is functioning well.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: Singapore companies are already learning to adapt to this new type of human resource (HR) structure.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: The company's workforce should comprise the old, middle-aged and young; each age group has its special qualities and everyone's value should be appreciated.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: For example, when female employees go on maternity leave, and the male employees go for reservist training, perhaps the older workers who have been trained could help to hold the fort and help to share the workload.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: In my company, the oldest worker was 80 years old, who carried on working until he passed on two years ago.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: When we arrange his work, we do not expect him to exert himself, but he won the respect of colleagues from his experience and attitude.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: In fact, if the bosses treat their elderly workers well in the long term, it also becomes a form of encouragement to younger employees.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: If they see this being practised in the company, the younger employees would have greater confidence in the company and give them a greater sense of belonging.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: Those businesses which are in the process of restructuring, especially those in traditional industries, need to think of ways to adapt to new business environments.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: From the viewpoint of economic development, the Government encourages enterprises to innovate and bring in new technology to create more benefits.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: From the viewpoint of social development, the Government requests enterprises to take care of the older workers and arrange for suitable positions for them.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: But at the same time, the Government needs to be aware that business costs are rapidly rising and understand the predicament of businesses.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: Our trade growth will continue to remain weak.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: Under these economic situations, it is very difficult for companies to seek growth.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: More companies are struggling to survive and are trying very hard to transform.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: Thus, I hope that when the Government rolls out its policies, Ministries should be even better coordinated and make policies more relevant.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Deputy Speaker, Sir, I support the Retirement and Re-employment (Amendment) Bill.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This is good news for our mature workers, especially those above the age of 62 and who wish to continue working for as long as they can.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Our employment practices and workforce need to evolve to meet the challenges of the future global economy and job trends.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The intrinsic value of mature workers is the invaluable wealth of experience they bring with them, which companies can tap on when training their younger workers.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: It makes business sense to re-employ them beyond 62, if they are fit and capable to handle the demands of the job, and I am glad that Mr Thomas Chua agrees to this point as well.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: As Executive Secretary of the National Transport Workers' Union (NTWU), I am heartened that our public transport operators were among the first to raise the retirement age of their workers beyond 62.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Some of these mature bus drivers have driven more than 30 bus routes throughout their careers and this makes it easier for the operational team to deploy them to service different bus routes, especially during emergencies.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Our public transport operators also assign experienced bus captains to guide new bus captains.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Newer and younger bus captains have told me that they pick up useful skills like providing better service and learnt life skills like work ethics and job dedication from their seniors.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: These benefits of hiring mature workers are especially more salient in industries with manpower challenges, like the bus service industry.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Today, many companies are already re-employing their mature workers beyond the re-employment age and I look forward to seeing even more companies hire workers beyond age 67.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Age should not be a limit, but be a quality valued by employers.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Within the Labour Movement, we know of many companies that do not cut the wages of their 60-year-old employees.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Some continue to receive salary increments due to their good performance.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This legislative change sends a strong signal that companies should pay their workers based on performance, regardless of age.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: For those approaching retirement age, having a fair remuneration package would encourage more to consider working so that they can remain financially independent, enjoy leisure activities, save up for retirement and be prepared for any unexpected medical expenses.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Lastly, we need to ensure that our workplaces are age-friendly.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Creating age-friendly workplaces requires a whole-of-organisation approach, with open dialogues between employers, unions and all employees.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Areas of work that can cause strain on our mature colleagues should be identified and promptly addressed.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The JR Grant aims to make current jobs physically easier, safer and smarter through improvements to the workplace environment or work processes to increase workers' productivity and satisfaction.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: With assistance from the Singapore Industrial and Services Employees' Union (SISEU), Aerospace Component Engineering Services Pte Ltd is one of the first few companies to embark on this enhanced grant administered by NTUC's U Live department.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Previously, workers were required to engrave intricate details like 2D dot-matrix or QR prints on very small data plates.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Thanks to job redesign, workers can now make use of a laser marking machine and the relevant software to perform the engraving.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This is especially helpful for the mature workers as it augments their physical abilities and enables them to continue doing this high precision job.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This also helps them gain new skills and new process capabilities.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The reduction in printing errors saved time and money, thus raising productivity for the company.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This example showcases the viability of job redesign and I urge the Ministry to encourage and support more companies to embark on such projects.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: It would also go some way to address Mr Thomas Chua's concern about rising business cost.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I would also urge more companies to offer free health screening to their mature workers and encourage more workers to take ownership and adopt a healthier lifestyle.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Through a health screening jointly organised by NTWU, Health Promotion Board and SBS Transit, 65-year-old Senior Bus Captain Mr Lee Chai Seng found that he had a high level of triglycerides and high blood pressure.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Besides medication, he was advised to make lifestyle and dietary changes.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: After exercising regularly, reducing his food intake and opting for healthier meals, Mr Lee obtained a clean bill of health from the doctors within a year.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: A healthy worker is a happy and better worker who can contribute to his or her company.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: More companies should recognise that this is a win-win.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: It is crucial that they are recognised and supported at the workplace.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Employers, with support from our Government agencies, can lead the way to redesign jobs to make full use of the wealth of experience and abilities of our mature workers.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We need a real mindset and culture change to get rid of ageism at the workplace.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: With that, Mr Deputy Speaker, Sir, I support the Bill.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Reiterating Minister of State for Manpower Mr Sam Tan during the Committee of Supply debates last year, this is a necessary move which shows that Singapore is not just accepting, but embracing our older workforce.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The retention of manpower will inject vitality into our tight labour market.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: At the same time, we are helping older Singaporeans to remain employable.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My personal interactions with residents in Nee Soon, which has a sizeable population of seniors, tell me that many still want to work because of their desire to be financially independent, and many are already working well beyond the age of 65.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: By raising the re-employment age, we will shine a light on the value that older workers can bring to our workplace, fostering a mindset shift that ageing is not a burden, but an opportunity.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This Bill provides further flexibility for companies, while offering greater options for older workers.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: However, as we recognise this group of seniors who work only because they want to, we must not forget the population of seniors who work because they have to.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: For many of the seniors, the reality is that they do not have enough savings to retire.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I have met many who continue to work despite physical illness and severe fatigue.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Even for those with children, for some, financial contributions from their children are insufficient for their basic survival and I have encountered a few residents in Nee Soon East whose children only provide for them because the law mandates so, through the Parents Maintenance Act.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This would be a very sad reflection of Singapore, if we are a society that cannot even offer rest and repose to our people during their final days.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: There are distinct differences between these two groups and a better understanding of this landscape can help create better policies.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
