text: I certainly hope there will be more enlightened employers who will provide these older workers employment beyond 67 and certainly envision a day when the retirement age can be raised to 65 and re-employment could continue without a cap in age as long as a person is mentally well and physically fit to work and can contribute effectively and, more essentially, continue to embrace lifelong learning taking a three "A"s approach, that is, "Adopt, Adapt and Advance".

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: However, it is lamentable that there is still a negative perception amongst employers that older workers are a liability to the company.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Many employers plainly label older workers as too old for the job, lacking in energy and creativity, are not tech-savvy, have health problems and not able to work long as there are uncertainties in their health condition.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: If one were to flip the coin to the other side, one would come to realise that, fundamentally, older workers provide stability to the organisation.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: For example, should the network fail or if there is tech downtime, they do not panic for they have alternative ways to get things done even though they are not tech-savvy, unlike our younger generation who often become paralysed when there is tech downtime.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: We should recognise and acknowledge the fact that our Baby Boomers and Generation X are willing to learn new technology to be tech-savvy.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Our older workers work in an era when work-life balance means work until the job gets done.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: For employers to recruit and retain them, it is all about the art and science of managing older workforce which companies must embrace.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: We need to address the plight of our older workers, especially those above 65 who have lost their job prior to the legislation and now seeking employment.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: It is a great challenge, indeed, for this group of Singaporeans to find a job.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Also with the slowing economy, what safeguards can we provide these older workers who are eligible for re-employment but lost their job because of early termination of term contract when companies underperform since older workers, besides foreigners, are the first to be terminated?

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: There is unspoken discrimination which is, indeed, difficult to establish.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Anecdotally, there are many older workers, especially those beyond 65 who increasingly find it a challenge to even be given an opportunity for interview.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: PMEs especially, who have lowered their expectations, do see a constant roadblock with age being the undeniable barrier.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: A technician denied  re-employment after he turned 65 since the employer's legal obligation is until employee is aged 65, sought employment in many industries, including the security industry, which was a 12-hour shift work.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: He wants to be gainfully employed so as to keep himself active while earning to support his spouse who is a housewife as his two children are residing overseas.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: The word is to keep himself active, that is, occupied, and to have some money in his pocket for daily expenses. "Is it too much to ask for?" he asked.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: He personally shared that there is prejudice against older workers which is a challenge to prove as it is rather subtle.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: I shared with him that TAFEP has been doing extensive work to promote fair and progressive work practices and to highlight cases of such nature to TAFEP should he feel strongly that there is discrimination.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: He shared that he does not want trouble.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: I believe there are many of such cases where people are trying to get an employment and subsequently stop trying as it produces futile outcomes.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: I wish that all employers, be it multinational corporations (MNCs) or SMEs, as part of their corporate social responsibility, can be enlightened, be fair and inclusive by providing a suitable job and a flexible work arrangement to allow for older people to be economically viable and self-sustaining.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: From the health and economic perspective, it is also good for the nation and the society as a whole.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: I certainly hope MOM can provide more effective and sustainable incentives and continue promoting and sharing good practices of companies that hire older workers.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: As we see the ageing population growing rapidly, perhaps it is worthy for the Government to consider creating cottage industries for the greying population.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: This, indeed, will require a tripartite effort to create genetic mutation of Singapore's DNA of how individuals view ageing and that to cultivate a culture of "age neutral workplace" as well as "age-friendly workplace".

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: It is all about attitude, skill and adaptability.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Technology can complement the effort of these older workers without having to totally replace them.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: We often hear of companies employing foreign workers at the expense of older workers.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: This is where monitoring and enforcement are required to deal with such unscrupulous employers and such sensitive issues.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Lastly, on the revision of the Bill itself, I would like to seek a few clarifications.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: One, with reference to section 7 of the principal Act, it is good to include the tripartite guidelines as a reference in this Act where the explicit details are contained in the guidelines.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: For example, the need for the employer to inform the employee of its intention to reemploy at least three months before the employee turns 62.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Even if these guidelines are referenced elsewhere but for greater accessibility and quick reference, I would urge MOM to consider this suggestion.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Two, with reference to section 7A of the principal Act section (d), subsection (4) section (e) and sub-section (6), does this amendment mean that reemployment contracts will not be deemed as a new contract and employee's employment can be considered as a sail through?

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: In the amendment under section 7B(5) also provides for the continuity of the employee's service for the purpose of computing the employee's entitlement to annual leave and sick leave.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Would not this mean that subsection (1) is not as relevant?

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Can they be expected to seek such employment opportunities among their parent/subsidiary companies with this amendment?

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: I am indeed heartened that being old in Singapore will increasingly be less of a liability from the employment perspective.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: As we mature as an ageing society, it would be notably worthy for MOM to keep track of gender-based re-employment data so that there can be a more targeted effort to increase employment amongst older Singaporeans.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: As our population ages, we can expect to live longer and work until much older.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: During my house visits and at my Meet-the-People Sessions (MPS), I have come across middle-aged residents who have expressed their worry at imminent job restructuring, salary reduction or employment retrenchment.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: For some of them, even though they are in their 50s, they are still supporting young school-going children as well as elderly parents.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: On top of that, they are still paying off their home loan.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Yet another group of middle-aged residents are the sole breadwinners for their families, and job insecurity as well as salary reduction weigh heavily on their minds and shoulders.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I particularly support clause 11(2), (3) and (4) to repeal section 5 of the principal Act.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This is good news and is very fair to our senior employees.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I believe that once someone reaches the age of 60, it does not mean that that person is less competent or less able to work.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Competency and the ability to work really depends on the individual, regardless of age.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Besides, with life expectancy now expected to be between 80 to 85, being 60  is still considered relatively young.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: A 60-year-old would still have a good 10-15 years to work and be economically active.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: There is, however, Mr Deputy Speaker, one part of the amendment that I am concerned about.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: One month's notice, which is standard practice, may seem like a reasonable period.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: But for those who are older, say, 50  and above, one month may not be enough to find another job.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I have met older residents who have lost their jobs and are unable to find another job even after many months of searching, sending out job applications, attending interviews, and even after undergoing skills training in new areas of specialisation.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Some have even resorted to settling for lower-paying jobs or taking up jobs that do not fully utilise their skills or allow them to tap on their past work experience, because they are quite desperate to find another job, any job, just so that they can continue to pay their bills and support the family.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This is an area in which I hope we can work closely with employers in providing more opportunities for older workers to undergo proper work redesign to ensure job relevance or provide them with more time to gain alternative employment.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: (In Malay):   The amendments to the Retirement and Re-employment Act are a welcome move, especially the move to repeal section 5 of the principal Act.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The repeal of section 5 will give more assurance to workers and employers that one's age should not be used as a yardstick to measure whether someone is capable, is still able to work or is still competent for the job.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Therefore, employers are no longer able to reduce an employee's salary just because he or she has reached the age of 60.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Personally, I have met those who are in their 20s but cannot endure hard work and cannot accept criticism at the workplace.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: At the same time, I have acquaintances who are above 60  but are still working actively, even though they have heavy work responsibilities and have to endure long working hours.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: For so long, our community has become comfortable with the notion that 55 is the retirement age.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: But in reality, with higher standards of living and life expectancy now reaching age 80 to 85, the age of 55 is still relatively young.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: A person who is 55 can still work and be active for 10, 15 or 20 years more.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Here, I would like to urge our Malay community to avoid planning their retirement too early.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Employment is meaningless if we are unable to spend time with our family or pursue personal interests or perform our religious obligations.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I believe we have heard of celebrities like creator of Marvel Comics Stan Lee, fashion designer Vera Wang and founder of GAP fashion retailer Donald Fisher.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: They became famous and embarked on new careers at the age of 40.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Our own countryman, Mr Sarkasi Said, a batik master whom I respect deeply, also began to enjoy success in his field at the age of 40.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Although Mr Sarkasi is now 76 years old, he is still actively practising the art of batik making.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I am reminded of the saying "Life Begins at 40".

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Maybe it is also because I am now 40, too.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: But as long as we breathe, we should continue working and serving our nation, society and family.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: (In English): We need to showcase more older employees who are contributing extensively to their employers and companies and value-adding to their work despite their age.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Such open-minded and inclusive employers who employ them should also be showcased and commended for retaining, retraining and re-employing older workers.

speaker: Mr Heng Chee How (Jalan Besar)
text: We must continually innovate our methods so that our mature workers can keep contributing, and this Bill does that.

speaker: Mr Heng Chee How (Jalan Besar)
text: Second, big disruptions are happening to global trade, technology, business models, buying behaviour.

speaker: Mr Heng Chee How (Jalan Besar)
text: How things are made, sold and bought are all changing quickly.

speaker: Mr Heng Chee How (Jalan Besar)
text: Businesses and workers who can adapt will grow.

speaker: Mr Heng Chee How (Jalan Besar)
text: Those who cannot, risk becoming obsolete more quickly than before.

speaker: Mr Heng Chee How (Jalan Besar)
text: These same factors will also impact the chances of displaced workers when they look for jobs.

speaker: Mr Heng Chee How (Jalan Besar)
text: Hence, my view is that improvements in this Bill are absolutely necessary but are not sufficient to maximise the working years of mature workers who would have to deal with this increasing flux.

speaker: Mr Heng Chee How (Jalan Besar)
text: This brings me to my third point, which is that there is a critical need for the tripartite partners to examine these developments carefully and proactively devise policies and plans to address them in the interest of both mature workers and Singapore.

speaker: Mr Heng Chee How (Jalan Besar)
text: Very few employers had resorted to that, given that most were fair-minded and that pay is very much performance-driven nowadays.

speaker: Mr Heng Chee How (Jalan Besar)
text: This gives more flexibility and scope for job sourcing.

speaker: Mr Heng Chee How (Jalan Besar)
text: However, it is important to note that it is the worker's right whether to accept such an offer, and they cannot be ridden roughshod over.

speaker: Mr Heng Chee How (Jalan Besar)
text: So, that retains the security that they have under current arrangements.

speaker: Mr Heng Chee How (Jalan Besar)
text: Where the offer cannot be met with acceptance, the worker remains entitled to EAP.

speaker: Mr Heng Chee How (Jalan Besar)
text: The Labour Movement fully understands our mature workers' feelings and needs and has been pushing hard for an early resolution.

speaker: Mr Heng Chee How (Jalan Besar)
text: Employers wanted added flexibility of options for them to fulfil their legal obligations without overly constraining their business and manpower decision-making.

speaker: Mr Heng Chee How (Jalan Besar)
text: Workers, on the other hand, wanted more legal assurance to help them work beyond 65 and on fair terms.

speaker: Mr Heng Chee How (Jalan Besar)
text: They do not want to be discriminated against just because of age.

speaker: Mr Heng Chee How (Jalan Besar)
text: In short, the negotiators were seeking a balanced and sustainable approach to achieve flexi-security.

speaker: Mr Heng Chee How (Jalan Besar)
text: The amendments proposed in this Bill are, therefore, agreed to as a package to address the needs and interests of both the mature workers and businesses.

speaker: Mr Heng Chee How (Jalan Besar)
text: A key lesson from these negotiations is that all sides were open to considering fresh approaches and innovations to reach a win-win outcome that secures each side's core interests.

speaker: Mr Heng Chee How (Jalan Besar)
text: Such a mindset would be even more necessary when seeking new paths forward in the future.

speaker: Mr Heng Chee How (Jalan Besar)
text: I now move on to my second point.

speaker: Mr Heng Chee How (Jalan Besar)
text: A company will only employ a worker when there is a need to create a job position and when they can find a candidate whom they believe is worth employing.

speaker: Mr Heng Chee How (Jalan Besar)
text: Even as we work hard to transform ourselves, we are buffeted by serious cyclical and structural changes.

speaker: Mr Heng Chee How (Jalan Besar)
text: Events in 2016, for example, have also shown us how volatile, uncertain, complex and ambiguous (VUCA) the world is becoming.

speaker: Mr Heng Chee How (Jalan Besar)
text: Consider the nationalist and protectionist backlash against globalisation and free trade, rapid currency swings, heightened global political instability, terrorist and cyber threats, technological changes interacting with social connectivity to upend business models in both manufacturing and services and to redefine where productivity and innovations are to be found and exploited.

speaker: Mr Heng Chee How (Jalan Besar)
text: So, these developments raise two questions, one I consider basic and the other one consequential.

speaker: Mr Heng Chee How (Jalan Besar)
text: The basic question is: given these disruptive challenges, how will goods and services be produced and sold?

speaker: Mr Heng Chee How (Jalan Besar)
text: If technology and social connectivity, whether through driver-less vehicles, 3-D manufacturing, robotisation or e-commerce, if these are causing the creating, selling and buying of goods and services to be carried out in very different ways from before, then just making laws to enable people to do existing jobs for more years would become less and less adequate for more and more people as time passes.

speaker: Mr Heng Chee How (Jalan Besar)
text: Even upgrading skills to do existing jobs better may or may not be adequate.

speaker: Mr Heng Chee How (Jalan Besar)
text: This flux increases the risk of mismatch and worker displacement.

speaker: Mr Heng Chee How (Jalan Besar)
text: The structural challenge in this is very real and serious.

speaker: Mr Heng Chee How (Jalan Besar)
text: Unless we ready ourselves to deal with it, structural unemployment, which is sticky, may rise.

speaker: Mr Heng Chee How (Jalan Besar)
text: And structurally unemployed workers, especially mature ones, will find that even cyclical upturns will not bring back the jobs because the old jobs may no longer exist.

speaker: Mr Heng Chee How (Jalan Besar)
text: The consequential question is: what should we then do to help mature workers stay employed or be re-employable in this changed and changing environment?

speaker: Mr Heng Chee How (Jalan Besar)
text: I believe that, for this, we need to strike out boldly in three areas.

speaker: Mr Heng Chee How (Jalan Besar)
text: First, measures that help mature workers stay valuable and cost-competitive.

speaker: Mr Heng Chee How (Jalan Besar)
text: In this regard, I note the Minister's point that this is being reviewed, and I strongly support every effort and consideration towards its extension because not only would it help render the mature workers more cost-competitive in general but, in the current soft economic climate, it would be particularly pertinent.

speaker: Mr Heng Chee How (Jalan Besar)
text: Next, increase publicity of mature workers being valued for their worth on the job, as well as for their resourcefulness and tenacity in adapting to new circumstances and in seizing opportunities.

speaker: Mr Heng Chee How (Jalan Besar)
text: The more our society sees this as normal, the more mindsets about mature workers ‒ who they are, what they are capable of ‒ will shift in the positive, correct and desired direction.

speaker: Mr Heng Chee How (Jalan Besar)
text: While this is true for workers of all ages, it would be particularly pertinent for mature workers of all levels, given the realities of the labour market.

speaker: Mr Heng Chee How (Jalan Besar)
text: To do this well, there is a need to significantly improve our knowledge of where the jobs and displacements of today and the future are or will be.

speaker: Mr Heng Chee How (Jalan Besar)
text: We also need to enrol the mature workforce into life-long adaptive upgrading much more intensively and find ways to guide such learning and relearning beyond providing funding.

speaker: Mr Heng Chee How (Jalan Besar)
text: Our job and training matching efficiency and effectiveness must also undergo a step upgrade to deal with the expected larger flow volumes as this flux spreads and intensifies.

speaker: Mr Heng Chee How (Jalan Besar)
text: It would also require significantly enhancing social support and lowering switching costs for displaced mature workers who are undergoing retraining for new jobs in new sectors.

speaker: Mr Heng Chee How (Jalan Besar)
text: These displaced workers have families to feed and commitments to meet.

speaker: Mr Heng Chee How (Jalan Besar)
text: So, if left without systematic transition support, many more may exhaust their resources and end up in sub-optimal and underemployed work.

speaker: Mr Heng Chee How (Jalan Besar)
text: Others may be discouraged from the labour market altogether and you will have this pool building up and that would become eventually a threat to social cohesion.

speaker: Mr Heng Chee How (Jalan Besar)
text: The third area of action would be the structural reform of work, work processes and also legislation, regulation and so on.

speaker: Mr Heng Chee How (Jalan Besar)
text: The gig economy and the workforce will grow quickly, if we look at international trends.

speaker: Mr Heng Chee How (Jalan Besar)
text: Companies will keep a small core and tap on contract, outsourced or freelance labour more and more frequently.

speaker: Mr Heng Chee How (Jalan Besar)
text: New-age workers and displaced ones may also seek to earn a living as self-employed, freelance providers, independent contractors, or other non-traditional forms of work, whether out of choice or no choice.

speaker: Mr Heng Chee How (Jalan Besar)
text: New technologies and social commerce platforms may also reduce or eliminate certain previously abundantly available self-employed or gig job options in time to come, such as the impact of autonomous vehicles on hired driving.

speaker: Mr Heng Chee How (Jalan Besar)
text: This is, therefore, much more complex than moving from full-time to part-time work, or moving from being a salaried worker to being self-employed as a business owner.

speaker: Mr Heng Chee How (Jalan Besar)
text: I mentioned the state for considerations, such as in terms of tax collection and social support outlays.

speaker: Mr Heng Chee How (Jalan Besar)
text: Press on to revamp workplaces and work processes to be age-universal, through ramping up such schemes as WorkPro.

speaker: Mr Heng Chee How (Jalan Besar)
text: The design of workplaces, work processes and jobs have a direct and significant impact on whether older persons can avoid premature loss of employability.

speaker: Mr Heng Chee How (Jalan Besar)
text: Given the relative difficulty faced by displaced mature workers in finding new jobs quickly, such upstream work will help reduce downstream pain.

speaker: Mr Heng Chee How (Jalan Besar)
text: At the same time, the future is rushing at us at an unprecedented speed and with unfamiliar manifestations.

speaker: Mr Heng Chee How (Jalan Besar)
text: Even as we strengthen our frameworks of today, we must mobilise Singapore and Singaporeans to tackle that VUCA future with focus, joint effort and a sense of urgency.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In view of our ageing population in which one out of four Singaporeans will be aged 65 and above by 2030, the Government would have to work with employers to adjust to the new norm where older workers will become one of the key pillars of our workforce.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The amendments to the Retirement and Re-employment Act are necessary to include those who are able and willing to continue working.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Raising the re-employment age to 67 is one thing; convincing companies to retain and recruit these senior employees is another.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We need to balance the needs of businesses and workers.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: How would the Government encourage both employers and employees to retain older workers at other jobs within the company and at re-negotiated wages?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: My concern is that it is easier for an employer to offer EAP than to help an older employee find a position.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: However, to attract employers to hire workers at the much older age of 67, particularly those who used to work at other companies, additional incentives, monetary or otherwise, would have to be given.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Incentives will be needed for the current transition period until the concept of working into a person's 70s or even 80s becomes more widely accepted and integrated into our company culture.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: What are their success rates and the percentages of such workers being retained and redeployed?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In addition, what is the percentage of older workers aged 62 and above in SMEs, relative to large corporates?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This information will be useful for reference by both the public and private sectors and will inform our future policy measures.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: I rise in support of this Bill as the amendments seek to help older local workers who are able and wish to stay employed to do so.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: With an ageing population, increasing life expectancy, we are seeing more people able and wanting to stay in the workforce.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: In my role as a Member of Parliament, I have met many older residents who have shared with me their desire to stay employed.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Raising the re-employment age to 67 years and the provisions in this Bill will be welcome news for these older workers.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: There are three areas of the Bill that I wish to clarify.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Over the last five years, we do see an increasing trend of older people working in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Can the Minister clarify what this will mean for those born before July 1952 who are currently employed and not yet 67 years of age?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: While I understand the need to give employers time to adjust to these changes, can those aged above 65 but below 67 be included to receive the same benefits with the provisions of this Bill as those born on or after 1 July 1952?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: The second area, the repeal of the provision allowing employers to cut employees' wages at the age of 60.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: I am glad that this provision is being repealed.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: It is only fair that employees, regardless of their age, should not be compensated any less for the job that they are doing just because they are older.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: The Minister has shared in his speech that the Government is assessing the need to extend the 3% additional SEC that supports employers to offset wages which will expire on 1 July this year.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: I do hope that a decision on this can be made sooner as it will benefit those currently working aged below 67 not covered by the new re-employment age of 67 as well as what the Minister had shared in his speech, those working and above 67.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: The final area, on the inclusion of the option to allow eligible employees to be re-employed by another employer to increase labour market flexibility, it is good to allow for this flexibility and also having the safeguard that this can only be effected with the agreement of the employee.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: I do believe that going forward, there is a larger factor that needs to be addressed, especially as we discuss older workers.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: With the speed of technological changes and the disruptions impacting industries, business models, how work is done and the type and quality of jobs available, there will be job creation, but also job displacements, as well as new skills requirements.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: So, while we make provisions for re-employment and raise the re-employment age to enable older workers to stay in the workforce if they wish and are able to, we need to complement this with concrete efforts to future-enable all workers.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: This will involve the development, training and retraining of workers before they reach 60.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: This will help workers, including older workers, to be more ready to take on re-employment opportunities and new roles that will exist at re-employment age.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: For workers, having a learning mindset is important.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: If all of this does not happen, we would probably see a situation where employers will have to make the EAP as the jobs available will not be suitable for the worker with the current employer or any other employer.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: For a society with an active workforce, surely our definition of retirement and re-employment must go beyond the traditional association with an age or the adjustment of benefits in a contract for older workers.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: A check with Oxford Dictionary describes retirement as "The action or fact of leaving one's job and ceasing to work".

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Literally, this means anyone can retire at any age they feel comfortable to go without a need for the job and not because they have reached a predefined age and need to be made redundant from work.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: I view both retirement and re-employment as personal choices where individuals decide when they wish to retire and whether they wish to be re-employed post-retirement at work and in what capacity.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Sadly, the current employment trends reflect the harsh reality of the mindset of many employers and society at large that links one's effective worklife contribution to a particular age.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: While we question the state of things, should we not be asking what the root cause is?

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: And are there better options in keeping a healthy, active workforce of willing and engaged workers?

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: I agree that it is necessary to have some short-term plans on creating active work for our seniors or Pioneer Generation.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: But is it sufficient to achieve sustainable re-employment through a transactional focus on areas like how and when companies find ways to employ our seniors beyond a certain age; or for the Government to continue providing transitional subsistence for the employers to hire our seniors?

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: However, depending on the Government alone or the law to ring fence and provide security for our older workers may be counter-productive in some instances and stagnates progression in achieving our desired outcome of having active ageing for those who wish to.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: There is a Chinese saying, 强 中 自 有 强 中 手、 一 山 还 有 一 山 高.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: What this means here is, whilst we can put some measures in place to ensure that our older workers remain employed, but the employers could also find more reasons and tactics to argue why they prefer not to have seniors in their workforce.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Second, the perceived higher cost of having older workers due to their need for more medical benefits and correspondingly more sick leave and time off work.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Third, many companies lack the ability and bandwidth to deploy resources with job match, redesign appropriate jobs and have little will to retrain and manage these workers.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: As the Government encourages and persuades the tripartite partners to re-employ older workers, I urge the Ministry to consider the following on grounds of immediate and long-term needs.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: The first area is the increased focus on contract workers and freelancers.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: I have previously raised in this House and would reiterate again the need to provide access to basic knowledge related to contracts, service agreements, common HR practices to all working age adults, so that they are better equipped with understanding the latest industry practices and mentally prepared to handle the situation if it does arise.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Increasingly, our older workers will not be hired as permanent or full-time staff and more PMEs are facing retrenchments even before the specified retirement age.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Many of them end up with roles as part-time contract workers and freelancers.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Such information and knowledge bear significance and are central to the workers on being better-informed and reduces the risk of unfair practices or litigations.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: With the tightening labour market and a maturing workforce, it is hard to imagine why our older workers are perceived to bring no value at all to the workforce.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Some claim that physically, the older workers cannot cope or do not have relevant skills to handle the work.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: This may be true for some specific jobs, but it cannot be so for all.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Many companies are willing to hire fresh graduates or some with little relevant experience, so why not the older workers?

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: From my experience and observations, many mature workers have stronger resolve to learn, are willing to take on more scope if given the opportunities and share a greater sense of loyalty to their companies.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Indeed, their wealth of experience cannot be redundant simply because they have reached an age.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: To change this trend, I strongly urge hiring managers and employers to rethink and to shift their mindset.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Consideration must be based on the value that each worker brings to a company, many of which will not diminish with age, such as expertise and experience; and if done in collaboration, more work opportunities can be created locally and reducing social costs.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: In the second area, enhancing the framework for broad-based learning.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: We constantly speak about continuous learning and encourage individuals to cultivate a habit of learning not only in school but also at work.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Often, this is not an easy task for companies without a people development centric culture or others without the scale to offer their staff training beyond their current job scope.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: As we develop the scope of SkillsFuture in Singapore, I suggest looking at courses from a different angle and enhancing it in three ways.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Early exposure provides our students with choices and understanding of what the future work environment might be or to further pursue areas of studies they are keen to specialise in.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: For the companies, it is a resource pool and also an early recruitment of potential talents that fit their company well.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: While it is important to develop skills in areas that one is lacking and those where one is passionate about, the identification process and taking the relevant courses to reinforce it is not an easy path.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Some of the programmes can be on-the-job training or cross-function job rotations; and this ultimately benefits the companies and enhances broader skillsets of our workers over time.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: This will also assist the SMEs which usually do not have the luxury of more resources and ability to dedicate their staff for external training.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: For workers in this situation, they will be further disadvantaged from not having a chance to learn broadly.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: With time, they may even face more difficulties to find the next appropriate job.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: So, Mr Deputy Speaker, while I support the Bill and efforts that MOM has made thus far, we need to be cautious of the weary and prolonged effects a society may face if the efforts are made solely on the part of the Government.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: I hope our society can embrace the reality of an ageing workforce, progressively change their mindset on appreciating values of workers based on their abilities and make room for more people who are willing to contribute their part.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: I think that is a very good measure that many will welcome.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: The next challenge we face is to get the information across to both our seniors and our companies.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: More so for the former, as our seniors are much more vulnerable.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: One important point to communicate is the concept of re-employment age.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: On the ground, residents occasionally tell me that companies ask them to leave because they have reached "retirement age".

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Some companies even say that the "law prevents them from hiring seniors beyond a certain age".

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: I am disappointed when I hear such misconceptions.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: As my Parliamentary colleague Darryl David recently put it, as long as the employee is medically fit and willing, the re-employment age of 67 is just the floor and not the ceiling.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: This misconception shows us that empowering seniors with information is key.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: The ones for MediShield Life are very well-received and very effective.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Third, let us not forget social media, especially since some of our younger seniors are also tech-savvy.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Besides informing seniors, companies need to understand that they not only gain from monetary incentives, but also from the experience our seniors have.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: However, it is not easy for businesses, especially SMEs, to stay current on regulations.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Therefore, our Government can do more to keep our businesses informed.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: For example, one, the upcoming business grant portal can be clear in stating senior employment incentives and re-employment age, perhaps through a pop-up banner at the launch page.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: This will ensure that our business leaders and towkays are kept in the loop.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Two, the relevant MOM, CPF and Immigration and Checkpoints Authority (ICA) websites can display such information, too, so that the HR managers are aware of it as well.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: But for the law to see its intended effect, seniors and businesses need a genuine shift in mindset.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: And for that to happen, they must first be empowered with the right information.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: I look forward to the responses from MOM and I stand in support of the Bill.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: First of all, I am happy to see that all of us in this House share a common objective which is to help as many Singaporeans as possible to work for as long as possible.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Given the longer life expectancy, I think there is no disagreement that helping our seniors to live what I call "H2P2" − a Happy and Healthy, Productive and Purposeful life.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: I think we are on the same wavelength.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: The issue is: what is the best way to go about achieving this?

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Why do we not raise the retirement age?

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: The Member Assoc Prof Daniel Goh asked that question: why leave the retirement age at 62?

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Why not raise it to 65 or even higher?

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: We used to have a de facto retirement age of 55.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Later on, we formalised it at 60 and it was alright.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Later on, the tripartite partners worked very hard together to raise it to 62.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: First, the employers objected for the very obvious reason because they are concerned about the impact on businesses.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: On the part of the workers, Members may not be aware, our younger workers objected, too.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: In fact, at a grassroots dialogue chaired by Prime Minister Lee Hsien Loong, a young worker asked him a very direct question.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: He said, "I am now in my 40s.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: I have been waiting for many years to take over the position of my boss.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: My boss is going to retire very soon because he is reaching 62 soon.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Now, if you were to raise the retirement age to 65 and beyond, it means I have to wait a few more years." He asked, "How is the Government going to take care of the aspirations of the young?" The young employees objected.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Every time we raise the retirement age, employers will demand a wage cut because of various considerations, and the older employees would object to the wage cut.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Employers did not want to move, young workers did not want us to move, and unions were pressured by senior employees not to give in to demands for wage cuts.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: But we believe that instead of having all three parties looking at this as a problem, why not all of us work on a solution that can produce an all-win outcome?

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Every country talks about raising their retirement age but, in Japan, they pursued the direction of re-employment age.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: The core difference between retirement and re-employment age is that when you raise the retirement age, the expectation is for same job, same pay.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: As a result, we may deprive the younger ones of career progression.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Whereas when Japan introduced the idea of re-employment age, the concept is, not necessarily the same job, not necessarily the same pay.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: They told us when we visited them in 2005, 2006 that, in Japan, under the Re-employment Act, no manager is allowed to be re-employed as a manager so that the position will be made available to a younger successor, and that person who is re-employed will provide value-add, maybe as a consultant, an advisor, or a staff officer to guide and help the younger ones to succeed.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: In some cases, if the corporation does not have a position opening for them, they allow them to be deployed to the subsidiaries.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Because they can actually help to bring their expertise and experience to the subsidiaries.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: We thought it made a lot of sense.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: We invited the Japanese experts to come to Singapore to conduct workshops.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: And finally, we came to the conclusion that that is the best bet and the way to go ahead.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: As a result of that, we moved away from raising the retirement age towards the introduction of the re-employment age.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: I would say that, over the last five years since 2012, it has been proven that what we did was correct.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: The second point: are we moving too slowly?

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Deputy Speaker, Sir, we learnt from Japan the concept of re-employment.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: The re-employment age in Japan today is still at 65.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: We learnt from them five years ago and adopted the re-employment age of 65.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Our re-employment age at 67, compared to many other countries, is already among the higher ones.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Of course, some many argue: why not do away with retirement age completely?

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Why not do away with re-employment age completely?

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: There are countries that have no retirement age, for example, the UK, Australia, the US, Denmark, New Zealand and Germany.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: They have no retirement age, but yet at the same time, there are other countries − I am talking about the developed economies − they have a retirement age.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: For example, in Korea, it is 60; in Switzerland, 65 for males, 64 for females; Sweden, 67; Finland, 68; Luxembourg, 68.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Some of them are about the same as us, some are lower, and some are higher than us.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: At the end of the day, we look at the employment rates.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Yes, you can do away with the retirement age or have a higher or lower retirement age.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: The bottom line is: to what extent are we able to help the older workers to stay employed?

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: We looked at the employment rates of those who are aged 65 to 69, and guess what?

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Of the developed countries, two countries are higher than us: Korea whose rate is 44.8%, and Japan whose rate is 41.5%.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: We learnt from them about the re-employment age but when it came to actual employment rates, they are still higher than us.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: If we compare ourselves to all the other countries with a higher retirement age, for example, Luxembourg, their employment rate for those aged 65 to 69, is 7.1%, less than 10%.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: In the case of Finland, the retirement age is 68, but their employment rate for those aged 65 to 69 is 13.1%.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: In the case of Sweden, the retirement age is 67 and their employment rate is 21.9%.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: The UK has no retirement age, employment rate for those aged 65 to 69 is 21%; Australia, 25%; the US, 31%; and Denmark, 15%.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Eventually, what we hope is that our people can actually continue working for as long as they are able to, and as long as they want to.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Looking at the employment rate for those aged 70 to 74, Singapore is 24%.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Again, if we compare it to all these other countries, one country that is much higher than Singapore is Korea, which has 32.3%.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: I must really visit Korea soon to see how and what we can learn from them.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: But all the other countries are significantly lower.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: In other words, if we compare the employment rates of older workers aged 65 to 69, and 70 to 74, the tripartite partners in Singapore are very convinced that the way we are doing it is the right way.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: At the same time, we are not progressing too slowly.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: In fact, compared to other countries, our re-employment age at 67 is comparable and in fact, higher than many other countries, either going by the re-employment age as in Japan, or the retirement or pension age in other countries.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Therefore, I want to appeal for the support of Members: let us commit ourselves.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: At the end of the day, here in Singapore, what is our objective?

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: We want to ensure that our economy can continue to grow.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: We all recognise that for economic growth, we have to support businesses.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: However, the main objective, the end outcome of economic growth must be translated into employment opportunities for people, young and old, all inclusive.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Jobs represent the best welfare; full employment is the best protection.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Therefore, we will continue to evolve the re-employment model and, at the same time, make sure that our re-employment model in Singapore must be both pro-business and pro-worker.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: If we do not address the interests and concerns of businesses, we will eventually run out of jobs.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: But yet at the same time, if we do not take care of the interests of our workers, our people will eventually not be able to continue to pursue and live a "H2P2" life.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: With that as a backdrop, I will now address some of the points brought up by Members.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: A related issue is about the CPF Payout Eligibility Age (PEA).

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh asked whether we can roll back PEA from 65 to 60.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: For Member Louis Ng, he asked: with the increase in our re-employment age, does it mean that we are going to adjust the PEA to 67 as well?

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Deputy Speaker, Sir, let me explain the current situation.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Up until 2012, the link between the retirement age and CPF PEA was direct and identical.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: So, when the retirement age was 60, PEA was 60.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: When the retirement age went up to 62, PEA was 62.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: The increase in our PEA is already something like six years lagging behind the re-employment age.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: At the recommendation of the CPF Advisory Panel, we amended the rules by which members can draw on their CPF payouts.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Starting from 1 January 2016, CPF members will start their CPF payouts between ages 64 and 70.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Therefore, the relationship between re-employment age and the age of starting the CPF payouts has already changed.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: It used to be point-to-point, but now, it is a range.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: The CPF payout start range is now 64 to 70, and the re-employment age will be 67 by July, within that age band.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Next year, the CPF payout start range will be 65 to 70, and again, the re-employment age at 67 is still within that band.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: There is no longer a direct point-to-point linkage.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: I think on this, we are all in agreement.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: But one point which we are still in strong disagreement is really not about the de-linking, but rather, it is about whether we should reset the PEA back to 60.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: For this Government, we think it will be the wrong thing to do, given that the life expectancy of our people is getting longer.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Also on the point about letting our CPF members withdraw more money so that they can invest on their own.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: If Members have been following all the developments, many of the CPF members who had invested their money on their own through the CPF Investment Scheme, or CPFIS in short, have not done better.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Therefore, I believe that it is to the best interests of our CPF members for them to keep their CPF retirement money in CPF LIFE.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Please also do not forget that CPF members can withdraw their savings above the Basic Retirement Sum (BRS) if they already have got a sufficient housing charge or pledge in place.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: In other words, we are not depriving our CPF members from investing their own retirement sum, if they have anything above the BRS for those who have sufficient housing charge or pledge and above the Full Retirement Sum for those without sufficient housing charge or pledge.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Therefore, this amendment Bill is about raising the re-employment age.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: It has nothing to do with the CPF PEA or payout start range which, as I have said, is already fixed at 64 to 70 this year, and 65 to 70 from next year.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: If the employer says this worker is not eligible for re-employment due to poor performance, it is for the employer to show proof.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: If the employer says that this worker is not eligible for re-employment due to medical reasons, it is for the employer to show proof.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Some Members asked, "What if this company has no performance appraisal system in place?" When that happens, we will tell the employer, "Since you don't have proof, you don't have a performance appraisal system in place, and you don't have proof that this person has not been performing well, year after year, and more than that, along the way, you had not been giving him feedback, suggestions and so on, these cases would be ruled as being unreasonable denial of re-employment".

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: In the case of discrimination, I share the concerns of Members.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: This is something that we are always on the lookout for.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: For example, can the employer try to find ways to get rid of a worker just before 62?

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: A worker may come to MOM to complain and say, "I have been working for this company for 10, 20, 30 years; everything went very well.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: But somehow, three years before I turn 62, everything turned negative." If this worker is a union member, we can ask him or her to approach the union.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: If he is not a union member, he should come to MOM.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Regarding the employees' entitlement on re-employment, again, this is a trade-off between being pro-business and pro-worker.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: The tripartite partners negotiated and decided to strike a balanced outcome, which is that the core entitlement of workers provided for under the Employment Act should be protected.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: For example, paid sick leave of 14 days for outpatient consultation and 60 days of hospitalisation are protected.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: In the case of annual leave, the minimum seven days provided for under the Employment Act, again, is protected.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Some other entitlements may no longer be relevant and so, they are removed.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: It is unlikely that the re-employed workers would need maternity leave.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: The question, really, is what about the contractual benefits: medical benefits and other benefits?

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Contractual benefits have never been part of the Employment Act.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: In other words, even the Retirement and Re-employment Act cannot protect your contractual benefits.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: It applies to all workers, young and old.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Whether you are 40 years old or you are re-employed and aged 62, all your employment contract terms depend on what is contained in there; it is a subject of direct negotiation between the employee and employer, or between the union and the management.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: However, the tripartite partners are still concerned that the older workers, those who are re-employed, may not be in a good position to negotiate for fair terms and conditions.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: As a result, we have issued a set of tripartite guidelines.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: The latest revision will be issued later today.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: In these guidelines, we will highlight what are considered reasonable terms and conditions.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: These guidelines are very important because in the situation of any dispute, the employee can come to the Tripartite Alliance for Dispute Management (TADM) for mediation and come to MOM for mediation.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: If the mediation is not successful, the case can go to the Employment Claims Tribunals (ECT).

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: ECT will make reference to this set of tripartite guidelines.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: So, if the employer is, indeed, being unreasonable in terms of the terms and conditions and, after mediation, we could not succeed in a resolution and the case goes to ECT, ECT will make reference to this set of tripartite guidelines and rule whether the terms and conditions offered upon re-employment are reasonable.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: I want to assure Members of this House that the tripartite partners take this very seriously.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: On the issue of a new option for a second employer, some Members are concerned about what would happen if the second employer is not able to fulfil the commitments of the first employer.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: So, they asked if there is a way out for the second employer.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: First, I want to assure the Members that the consensus of the employee is a mandatory condition.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: If the worker does not feel comfortable, then he does not have to accept this offer.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Once the offer is accepted, the second employer will have to fulfil all the obligations of the first employer.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: For example, a Member mentioned about what would happen after one year, the worker is subsequently not offered re-employment at 63, after having been offered re-employment at 62.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: At the point of 63, if the worker is not offered re-employment, the second employer would have to pay the worker EAP.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Before the second employer can offer to pay EAP, the tripartite partners will come in to scrutinise whether this is the last resort.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: We will be monitoring very closely to ensure that there is no abuse of EAP.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: The large majority does not have this issue of abuse of EAP.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: As such, we believe the second employer will be tightly bounded by these criteria and conditions.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Mr Zainal Sapari asked if the notice period can be one year.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: We think that is sufficient but let us do more.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: On the payment of EAP, I agree fully with Mr Patrick Tay that we must have a safeguard in place to prevent abuse.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: As I mentioned, we watch it very carefully, and so far, so good.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: In terms of the review of the quantum of EAP, we just reviewed it this round.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: We take business concerns very seriously because we recognise that re-employment can only work if it is a win-win outcome.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: We have been in very close consultation through SNEF to take into account all the feedback.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: We will continue to provide support, not just through this scheme, but through the overall package that is coming up.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Ms Jessica Tan asked whether we can do something to help and encourage employers to re-employ the older workers, including those not eligible for re-employment till 67.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: The answer is yes, we are actively looking into this.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: The decision on the extension, what form, what coverage of this additional wage offset will be decided soon, well ahead of the 1 July implementation date.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Last but not least, I share the views of many Members here that at the end of the day, the true success of re-employment depends a lot on how we value our older workers and how we redesign their jobs.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: I am very happy to hear the Labour Members repeating the call for "ESS", or making our jobs "Easier, Safer, Smarter".

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Last year, we enhanced WorkPro for job redesign.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: I am still looking for more ways to encourage greater adoption.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Many countries have done something, so there is a lot that we can learn from.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Mr Melvin Yong asked about whether the Public Service can take the lead on re-employment.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Actually, the Public Service was the first one to adopt the re-employment age of 67 way back in January 2015.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: It has been about two and a half years ahead of the law.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: I also agree with Mr Heng Chee How that we should look at different ways to make "progressive workplace practices" more prevalent across the board.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: I also want to assure the Members that many of their good suggestions will be taken note of by the tripartite partners and will be incorporated in our implementation.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: At the end of the day, just because we have succeeded in re-employment in the first five years, from 2012 to now, it does not mean that the way forward will be smooth.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: The tripartite partners are concerned that as we raise the re-employment age, the higher the re-employment age, the more challenging it is going to be.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Therefore, we have to find ways on the one hand, to make sure that the workplace becomes more age-friendly so that the older workers will be able to remain productive and help companies to remain competitive; at the same time, we must also take good care of our older workers in terms of employability and welfare.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: We believe that by working together, we can continue to ensure that employment rates of our people aged 65 to 69, 70 to 74 and above, will always be among the highest in the world.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: First, with regard to the possibility of discriminatory employment practices, the Minister cited an example of ageism, everything going bad in the last three years and how the employee in that case can go to MOM.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: My question is: what will MOM do at that point?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: I suppose MOM will look at the case and see if it contravenes the Retirement and Re-employment Act.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: Would MOM also look at that company in a more systematic way?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: The reason I mention this is because of the "double weak companies".

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: For those who discriminate against Singaporeans, there is a so-called framework where you look for other evidence or a pattern of discrimination, who are the people they have hired over time and so on.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: Does MOM do that now in cases of ageist discrimination and other kinds of discrimination, or will it consider doing so in the future if it does not do so now?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: The second and last question is: the Minister talked about the link between countries which have a higher or no retirement age and the labour force participation of those aged 65-plus.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: I am wondering: why do the tripartite partners feel that raising the retirement age or eliminating the retirement age reduces the labour force participation?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: I am wondering if there is really a causation or could it just be a correlation.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: There could be other reasons countries like the UK and the US may have lower post-65 labour force participation; they could have more generous defined benefits and pension schemes, for example.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: It may not be just the raising of the retirement age that is the thing that lowered the labour force participation.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Of course, we will take every case seriously.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: I will not name this company but it is a company that I know.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: When we introduced re-employment up to age 65, the employees and the union asked the management how this would affect the renewal of the senior management in the company.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: The Chairman and CEO, in consultation with the top management of the company, about 20 to 25 of them, they came to a collective decision.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: They decided that in this company, all senior management of certain positions, on a voluntary basis, will exclude themselves from re-employment.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: They are very determined and said that leadership renewal for their company is critical to their sustained success.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: So, on a voluntary basis, they excluded themselves from re-employment.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: The difference between re-employment and retirement really is about mindset; about how are we going to be able to continue to address the concerns of businesses and, at the same time, also address the concerns of the younger workforce in terms of their career advancement; and, at the same time, address the concerns of the older workers for wanting to continue to be re-employed.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: So far, most countries still go for retirement age.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: To the best of our knowledge, Japan and Singapore are the only two on the re-employment model.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: The results, so far, I would say, seem to be more positive because the employment rates in Japan and Singapore are relatively higher compared to other countries.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: But the Member is right that this cannot be the only reason.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: It could be many other reasons and that is why in Singapore, we make sure that all the conditions are right, are conducive to be supportive of re-employment.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Through tripartite efforts, I believe we can continue to make progress.

speaker: The Chairman
text: The citation year "2016" will be changed to "2017", as indicated in the Order Paper Supplement.
